newsitem.title: FRANCE: Disputed Van Gogh masterpiece on sale in France.
newsitem.headline: Disputed Van Gogh masterpiece on sale in France.

text.p: One of Vincent van Gogh's last masterpieces goes under the hammer in Paris on Tuesday with the French state under pressure to buy the oil painting amid some suggestions it might be a fake.

Art experts reckon the Jardin a Auvers (Garden at Auvers), painted in July 1890 just before the Dutch artist's suicide, will fetch about 50 million francs ($9.5 million) at the Paris auction starting at 8.30 p.m. (1930 GMT).

That sum is only a quarter of its estimated value on the international art market. Its actual value was effectively cut by a contested 1989 ruling by the French Culture Ministry that the painting was a national treasure and barred it from ever leaving France.

The daily Liberation dubbed the work the "cursed painting" because of controversies over the export ban and media questions about the authenticity of the most accomplished oil painting from the last feverish days of Van Gogh's life.

"This is just a joke," auctioneer Jacques Tajan said of doubts about the painting, echoing the view of many art experts. "Of course this painting is by Van Gogh, as has been known since he painted it."
The painting, showing a garden full of swirling greens and blues with red flowers, was bought in 1992 by banker Jean-Marc Vernes for 55 million francs ($10.4 million) from collector Jacques Walter.
Walter successfully sued the state for imposing the export ban, arguing it slashed the painting's value at auction since his family acquired it in 1955.

The Supreme Court in February 1996 awarded Walter 145 million francs ($27.5 million) compensation -- 2.5 francs (50 cts) for each of France's 58 million inhabitants -- in a ruling that has dampened Paris's efforts to prevent the flight of other French masterpieces.
Many art lovers and commentators have said the state should now buy it outright.
"What might upset me the most would be that the state fails to buy this work," Tajan told France Info radio. "That would really be a slap in the face to the French taxpayer."
"There are two possibilities. You pay almost 150 million francs and you have nothing. You pay 50 million more and you have something the Musee d'Orsay is ready to hang in its galleries," he said.
Debate about the work's authenticity started with a critic of the conservative daily Le Figaro, Jean-Marie Tasset.

Tasset has argued the painting is too polished, does not feature in correspondence between Van Gogh and his brother Theo and that it might just come from a collection of a friend of Van Gogh, Claude Emile Schuffenecker, who copied masterpieces.
